statement: Some species reduce growth during reproduction.

scores.rationale: The stylized fact—that some species reduce growth during reproduction—receives clear conceptual and empirical support in DEB literature: the determinate-vs-indeterminate growth framework (snippets 3, 5) explicitly recognizes that growth stops during reproduction in some species, and several snippets describe slowed/plateauing growth at maturation in fish, turtles, and mammals (1, 10), trade-off models (8, 12, 18). However, a substantial set of snippets from the Froese/Pauly comment (2, 6) and Kear/Jusup (16) actively contradict the stronger claim that reproduction governs growth, arguing growth and reproduction occur sequentially rather than simultaneously, and DEB's own texts (7, 9) note that the onset of reproduction 'hardly seems to affect growth.' Because the fact is carefully hedged ('some species'), the evidence is moderate and the corpus is genuinely mixed/contested, so consensus is best rated neutral rather than fully corroborated.

No snippet contradicts the stylized fact; the remainder are off-topic or only tangentially related to growth/reproduction. The supporting evidence is moderate in strength but consistently aligned in direction, so the corpus corroborates the claim without conflict.

snippets.text: Abstract Early growth and environmental conditions can shape life-history trajectories. Long-lived iteroparous species with indeterminate growth face growth-reproduction trade-offs for most of their lives. Poor early conditions can delay primiparity and restrict growth, potentially compensated for by faster growth later in life, at the cost of reduced reproduction.

snippets.title: A New Look at Relationships between Size at Maturity and Asymptotic Size
snippets.label: supports
snippets.text: Comparative studies have revealed positive correlations between size at maturity and asymptotic size in several taxa with asymptotic growth after maturity. Using a simple growth model, we show that positive correlations between size at maturity and asymptotic size are predicted for different individuals in the same species if growth costs of reproduction are inversely related to size at maturity.

snippets.title: Probing of mortality rate by staying alive: The growth‐reproduction trade‐off in a spatially heterogeneous environment
snippets.label: supports
snippets.text: Abstract In many annual plants, mollusks, crustaceans and ectothermic vertebrates, growth accompanies reproduction. The growth curves of these organisms often exhibit a complex shape, with episodic cessations or accelerations of growth occurring long after maturation. The mixed allocation to growth and reproduction has poorly understood adaptive consequences, and the life‐history theory does not explain if complex growth in short‐lived organisms can be adaptive.

snippets.title: Size Matters: Individual Variation in Ectotherm Growth and Asymptotic Size
snippets.label: neutral
snippets.text: Body size, and, by extension, growth has impacts on physiology, survival, attainment of sexual maturity, fecundity, generation time, and population dynamics, especially in ectotherm animals that often exhibit extensive growth following attainment of sexual maturity. Frequently, growth is analyzed at the population level, providing useful population mean growth parameters but ignoring individual variation that is also of ecological and evolutionary significance.
